chief_complaint: visible layering of red blood inside the front chamber of the eye with blurred vision after being struck by tennis ball
hpi_details: 28M struck in eye by tennis ball presenting with pain and photophobia where slit-lamp reveals a 3 mm layered collection of red blood cells in the anterior chamber (Hyphema) requiring strict bed rest with head elevated 30 degrees, cycloplegics, and daily IOP monitoring to prevent secondary hemorrhage.
ideas: He thinks the impact of the tennis ball burst a blood vessel inside the colored part of his eye.
concerns: He is worried that the pool of blood inside his eye means he will permanently lose his vision or require emergency eye surgery.
expectations: He hopes an eye specialist can examine the eye immediately, relieve the pressure, and tell him his eyesight will be saved.

available_results.value: 3 mm layered collection of red blood cells in the anterior chamber

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Traumatic hyphema (blunt ocular trauma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Hyphema Blunt Ocular Trauma, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Traumatic hyphema (blunt ocular trauma).

Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.

dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Hyphema Blunt Ocular Trauma: visible layering of red blood inside the front chamber of the eye with blurred vision after being struck by tennis ball. 28M struck in eye by tennis ball presenting with pain and photophobia where slit-lamp reveals a 3 mm layered collection of red blood cells in the anterior chamber (Hyphema) requiring strict bed rest with head elevated 30 degrees, cycloplegics, and daily IOP monitoring to prevent secondary hemorrhage.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Hyphema Blunt Ocular Trauma.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Hyphema Blunt Ocular Trauma.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent ophthalmology assessment to exclude open-globe injury and monitor visual acuity and IOP. Protect the eye with a rigid shield, elevate the head, limit activity, and avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, and anticoagulants unless a treating clinician advises otherwise. Use cycloplegia and IOP-lowering therapy only as directed by ophthalmology; arrange close follow-up because rebleeding risk is highest in the first several days.

history.answer: I was hit directly in my right eye by a tennis ball a couple of hours ago, and now it is painful, blurry, and I can see blood pooling inside the front of my eye.
It happened suddenly about two hours ago during a tennis game; the pain and blurry vision began immediately, and the blood started settling at the bottom soon after.
It is only affecting my right eye; my left eye feels and sees completely normally.
The white of my eye is somewhat red, but what worries me most is a distinct line of red blood settled in the front chamber in front of my colored iris.
It is a dull, throbbing ache deep inside the eyeball, around a 6 out of 10 in severity.
My right eye is blurry and looks hazy with a reddish tint, although I can still see general shapes and count fingers.
Yes, looking at bright lights really hurts and worsens the throbbing ache in my eye.
I have not seen any rainbow halos around lights, and I do not have a headache, nausea, or vomiting.
There is only watery reflex tearing from the pain, with no yellow or green pus, stickiness, or crusting.
No, there is no itching at all.
There is a little bit of puffiness around my upper eyelid from where the ball hit, but no bumps or cuts.
Moving my eye makes it ache a bit more because it is sore, but I do not have double vision and my eye is not bulging out.
No, I haven't had a cold, runny nose, or cough recently, and no one around me has had an eye infection.
I do not wear contact lenses or prescription glasses.
A hard-hit tennis ball struck my right eye directly from close range at the net, and I was not wearing any eye protection.
No debris, metal, or chemicals entered my eye; it was solely the impact from the tennis ball.
I do not have seasonal allergies, hay fever, asthma, or eczema.
I do not suffer from dry eyes or dry mouth, and I was not staring at computer screens prior to playing.
I have no morning back stiffness, swollen joints, mouth ulcers, or bowel troubles.
I have no blisters or tingling on my forehead or nose, and I have never had shingles or herpes in my eye.
I do not take blood thinners or aspirin, and I haven't had any heavy coughing, vomiting, or straining.
I have never had any eye surgeries, serious eye injuries, or a diagnosis of high eye pressure or glaucoma.
I have never been diagnosed with sickle cell disease or sickle cell trait, and there is no sickle cell in my family.
The tennis ball hit me directly in the eye, so I figured the impact burst an internal blood vessel in my iris.
Seeing actual blood pooling in front of my pupil is terrifying—I'm scared I might go blind in that eye or need surgery.
I was hoping an eye doctor could look at this right away, check the pressure, and give me medication to clear up the blood.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, both diagnosed two years ago.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure; I haven't taken any ibuprofen or other painkillers today.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink one or two beers on weekends when socializing, nothing heavy.
I work in software sales and live in an apartment with my partner.
My father has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of eye diseases, glaucoma, or bleeding disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, oriented young male shielding his right eye from room light, in mild distress from ocular discomfort.
Mild ecchymosis and soft tissue swelling around the right upper eyelid and brow, with no lacerations or foreign material.
No step-off deformities, crepitus, or focal bony tenderness along the right orbital rims, zygoma, or maxilla.
Moderate ciliary flush and localized subconjunctival hemorrhage in the right eye, with an intact sclera and no dark uveal tissue prolapse.

Visual acuity is 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left, with a 3 mm layered meniscus of red blood cells in the inferior anterior chamber, a round sluggishly reactive pupil, a clear cornea without fluorescein uptake, and intact globe contour.
Intact light touch sensation over the ophthalmic and maxillary distributions bilaterally, with symmetric facial movements and normal extraocular motility.
